THE ALUMNI ASSOCIATION
By Laurance G. Wolfe, Rho '38
THE
ORIGIN of the Alumni Association
of Psi Upsilon�whose 25th year was
marked in 1957�Hes deep in the hearts of
brothers from every delegation since the
Fraternity's birth. It may be traced, too,
to chapter, local, and regional alumni
groups, many of which have shown sus
tained vitality since their inception. As a
matter of fact as
early as 1839 alumni of
the Theta, Delta and Beta chapters mani
fested their desire to continue ilieir under
graduate ties into postgraduate years by
holding annual alumni meetings in their
respective chapters halls. In 1851, ten
years before the Civil War, Psi U's repre
senting many chapters and Hving in Wis
consin organized an alumni body under the
name "Members of Psi Upsilon Fraternity
resident in the State of Wisconsin." Similar
alumni organizations sprang up on the west
coast, in the east, and in Chicago, in the
late 1870's. So on down through the years
other chapter and regional groups of
alumni took form.
Formal activation of the Alumni Asso
ciation as a national organization "to foster
in the Alumni a
continuing growth of their
love for and interest in the Fraternity and
the colleges and universities in which she
has chapters" occurred in 1932�on
April
9�at a
special meeting in the Hotel Gov
ernor Clinton, New York City.
It had been late in 1925 when Ed
win L. Garvin, Delta '97 (see front cover),
submitted a
proposal to Era! D. Babst,
Iota-Phi 1893, then President of the Ex
ecutive Council, suggesting the formation
of a national alumni body.
More than sixty alumni representatives
attended a
meeting called by the Execu
tive Council in 1926. The Annual Conven
tion of 1928 found alumni 300-strong in
attendance at an Alumni Convocation.
These brothers expressed earnest interest
in resuming a more active relationship with
the affairs of Psi Upsilon. The Executive
Council directed, after the Convention had
acted, that serious study and consideration
of the establishment of a national associa
tion be initiated. R. Bourke Corcoran,
Omega '15 and Charles P. Spooner, Rho
1894, gathered the facts upon which the
1931 Annual Convention based its instruc
tion to the Executive Council.
Brother Garvin, who had nurtured a
dream and moved to make it reality, was
appointed Provisional President of the
Alumni Association. He gave dynamic
leadership to a
program of informing chap
ters, local alumni associations and clubs,
and individual alumni throughout the
country, about the new association. Mem
bers, paying nominal dues, enrolled by the
hundreds.
Brother Garvin served as President of
the Alumni Association until 1933; Luke I.
Wilson, Mu 1895, was President until
1934. Others who have succeeded to the
top office of the national alumni group are
Benjamin T. Burton, Chi '21, Samuel L.
Rosenberry, Rho '23, Robert P. Hughes,
Delta '20, Charles H. Seaver, Psi '21 and
the current President, Alfred H. Morton,
Omicron '19.
The composition of the Board of Gov
ernors has varied over the years. Today
it is stronger than ever before since every
chapter except the Theta Epsilon of the
University of Southern California is repre
sented by an alumnus on the Board. At this
writing no alumnus of this chapter has
been found who is available to serve on
the board.
Early in its hfe, the Association set forth
some
worthy objectives for continuing ac
complishment. In general, these are:
1. The award of honorary society keys
to all undergraduates elected to Phi
Beta Kappa, Tau Beta Pi and Sigma
Xi as
part of a
thoughtful and com73

prehensive effort to improve scholar
ship throughout the fraternity;
2. The encouragement of local Alumni
Clubs manifested by assistance in
organization and extension;
3. The establishment of a central office
which serves as a
clearing house for
the entire fraternity and at which is
located what is undoubtedly the most
complete and accurate alumni list
ever assembled;
4. Constantly rendering assistance, fi
nancial and otherwise in connection
with various pubfications of the Fra
ternity, including song books, song
sheets, The Diamond and The An
nals; and in connection with the pub
lication of directories of living mem
bers of Psi Upsilon, to compile the
membership lists.
5. The establishment of an endowment
fund for the general welfare of the
Fraternity.
A study of the 1957 Report of the
Alumni Association is confirmation that
these initial programs have withstood the
test of the Association's first twenty-five
years. In his "President's Message,"
Brother Morton recorded the year's activi
ries of the six committees whose projects
bear most directly upon the original pur
poses of the Alumni Association. Portions
of Brother Morton's report are included
here since undergraduate brothers do not
receive the Alumni Association Annual Re
port. Committee accomplishments in 1957
included:
Undergraduate Awards and Scholarship
Committee: Maintained active correspond
ence with the undergraduate chapters with
Edwin L. Garvin, Delta '97 (center) is presented with a Life Membership Certificate in the Alumni Associa
tion by Alfred H. Morton, Omicron '19, President ofthe Association. Earl D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93, President
of the Executive Council when Brother Garvin first proposed a national alumn! group, adds his congratula
tions to Brother Garvin on the Association's 25th Anniversary.

cent years. In its
continuing effort to stim
ulate improved scholarship your Associa
tion reimbursed each winner of Phi Beta

cost of his key.
Office Management Committee: Effected

lication of the 1955 Directory, correct ad
dresses of some 4000 "lost" brothers were

ing 1955 Directory was found to be

vised the investment portfolio of the Asso

keeps the portfolio of securities under con
stant scrutiny.
Nominating Committee: Selected nomi

ception of the Theta Epsilon, is repre

ner of the New York Metropolitan Asso

to the encouragement from the national
group. More credit must
go, of course, to
the individual or individuals who, like
Brother Garvin, would not dismiss the
dream. The Alumni Association has a vital
desire to advance the ideals of Psi Upsilon
through local clubs and regional associa
tions. But the initiative and leadership for
such groups have always come from de
voted brothers who have been willing to
spend time and effort to provide a needed
spark. There are such regional alumni
groups now with headquarters in New
York, Chicago, Philadelphia, Boston, De
troit, Washington, D.C, Baltimore, Elmira,
Minneapolis, Montreal, Ottawa, San Fran
cisco, Los Angeles, Seattle and Portland.
Eleven of these had regular meetings
throughout 1957 and reported upon their
activities to the national association.
There are other ways in which the
Alumni Association has offered proof of
the contribution it makes toward fostering
the achievement of the Fraternity's ideals.
Of recent date, life members of the Asso
ciation have received an inscribed certifi
cate whose striking appearance invites
framing and display by its recipient. Mem
bership cards were sent to these members
and to those who are
dues-paying mem
bers. Such symbols of membership are
daily reminders to alumni of the sacred
bonds of Psi Upsilon's "singularly choice
brotherhood."
The Alumni Association has worked side
by side with the Executive Council and the
Annual Convention to create the Psi Up
silon Foundation. The educational endow
ment fund that will result was in the minds
of the Association's first planners. That this
idea is now
coming to fruition is a tribute
to the team-work of many alumni.
"The Alumni Association," Brother
Morton wrote in the 1957 Report, "is a
dynamic organization of serious purpose,
dedicated to preserving and stiengthening the well-being of our
fraternity from
the moment we cease
being undergradu
ates until 'the sands of life are run.'
"
In its first twenty-five years the Alumni
Association has indeed lived up to this
retioactive promise.

THE University of Rochester was
founded in 1850 as a small hberal arts
college for men.
Today it is a
private, giftsupported institution, which is non-de
nominational and coeducational, consisting
of the CoUege of Arts and Science, the
Eastman School of Music, the School of
Medicine and Dentistry, and University
School of Liberal and Applied Studies. In
September, three new schools, the College
of Engineering, the CoUege of Education,
and the School of Business Administration,
will be added. The University has a total
full-time enrollment of 3,500 students, with
an additional 3,000 part-time students.
It remained a liberal arts college for
men
only from its founding until 1900,
when, largely through the efforts of
Susan B. Anthony, the great women's rights
leader, women were admitted to the Uni
versity. The College of Arts and Science,
with an enroUment of 1850 undergradu
ates, is still the heart of the University. It
is located on the beautiful River Campus
on the Genesee River, adjacent to Genesee
Valley Park on the outskirts of Rochester.
The oldest division of the University
after the College of Arts and Science is
the world-renowned Eastman School of
Music, opened in 1921, which was built
and endowed by the late George Eastman,
founder of the Eastman Kodak Company.
The school has about 400 undergraduates,
and an additional 170 graduate students
working for master's and doctor's degrees.
It also has an extensive preparatory depart
ment.
Director of the School is Howard Han
son, noted conductor and Puhtzer prizewinning composer. Concerts are
presented
the year around by the various choral,
operatic and instrumental groups in the
School in the University's 3,300-seat East
man Theatie, one of the world's most
magnificent concert halls, and the more
intimate Kilbourn Hall located in the
School. Since its founding the School has
sought to encomage native composition by
presenting a series of orchestral concerts

devoted exclusively to the works of Ameri

large
number of American works have been
given performance, many of them for the

can Music each spring. The Rochester
Civic Orchestra is composed mainly of
Eastman School faculty members, and is
the nucleus of the Rochester Philharmonic
Orchestra, augmented by Eastman School

Opened in 1925, the School of Medicine
and Dentistry, one of the world's leading
centers of medical education, research and
treatment, was established through the
joint gift of the General Education Board
of the Rockefeller Foundation and Mr.
Eastman. The Medical Center, of which
the School is a
part, includes the two teach
ing hospitals. Strong Memorial and Roch
ester Municipal, a
psychiatric clinic, atomic
energy project, where research and teach
ing are conducted on medical problems
related to atomic energy production, under
contract with the Atomic Energy Com
mission, and a
Department of Nursing,
which has unusual faciUties for scientific
and clinical instruction. There are 285
medical students enrolled in the school, 230
nursing students, and about 100 students
on a
graduate level.
The University's extension division, Uni
versity School of Liberal and Applied
Studies, is organized to provide university
training to persons who are unable to at
tend one of the University's other schools,
or whose personal or
professional needs are
not met by the programs of such schools.
Classes are held in the late aftemoon, dming the evening, or on
Saturdays. Estab
lished in 1916, it was
reorganized in 1941
as
University School. It has over 3,000
full- and part-time students.
President of the University of Rochester
is Dr. Cornells W. de Kiewiet, formerly
acting president of Cornell, who became
Rochester's fifth president in 1951. He is
a noted historian, a native of Holland who

Among the noteworthy features introduced

lished in 1955, through which courses in

lations are offered, as well as a series of

Three new

tember, 1958, when the former divisions
of Education, Engineering and Business
Administration will be set up as the Col
lege of Education, College of Engineering,
and School of Business Administration,
each with its own Dean or Director and
awarding its own
degrees. The Institute
of Optics, the only university optical teach
ing and research department in the United
States offering complete ti-aining in geometiical, physical, and physiological optics,
was founded in 1938.
In 1957 it was decided to decentralize
much of the work leading to advanced de
grees, and at present each College or
School in the University is responsible for
its own master's degree program, instead
of under the former Graduate School. The
work for the degree Doctor of Philosophy
is under the general control of the Univer
sity Council on Graduate Studies.

By Dr. Charles J. Armstrong, Zeta Zeta '23

Brother Armstrong was a
guest speaker at the Zeta Zeta Graduation Banquet. His talk, "The
Forward Look," emphasized the need and importance of a liberal education as a means of under
standing and coping with everyday problems which occur in our democratic society. The copy of
this address came in too late to be used in full in this issue of The Diamond. Excerpts follow.]
Dr. Charles J. Armstrong, Zela Zeta '23
President of Pacific University
Graduation speeches are never easy things
to do, because they are traditional, and be
cause the speakers are
presumed to be those
who, from their own accumulated store of
wisdom and experience, can transmit useful
advice and chaUenging ideas to the young
people who at such a time are leaving behind
coUege days for the responsibiUties of the
wider world.
I am
by no means equal to such a task, nor
would I attempt it if I thought I were; for
if I have learned anything it is the fact that
one
generation is not disposed to profit either
by the sage advice or even
by the mistakes
of the previous generation. Young people
have their own ideas, they have their own
way to make, their own experiences to under
go: and that is the way it should be. Yet in
spite of this, there are some
positive values in
the educational process: your exposure to
the thoughts, the ideas and die aspirations
of men
through the ages, and to the record
of the past, your acquaintance with the physi
cal and biological aspects of the universe, give
you the means of understanding yourself,
your fellowman and the world in which you
live. Whether or not you choose to profit from
this intelligent comprehension is up to you;
herein hes the essential freedom of self which
is the most important single fact about man.
The record of the past is important not as
the dry and dusty bones of things long dead,
but because it illumines the present, and
casts what light there may be upon the fu
ture. We are what we are, and to a large
extent we will be what we become, because
of what mankind has said and thought and
done before. We cannot, for example, be
competent human beings or citizens if we
do not know the purpose of the humanities,
which is to enable man to understand man
in relation to himself.
. . . the ultimate goal of civilization is man
as an individual. Society exists, govemments
are instituted only to protect the rights, the
dignity, the sanctity of the individual. We
as citizens will forget this at our
peril.
Or again, think for a moment of the
splendid Greek civilization of two and a half
millennia ago; no
single culture has had so
much direct influence upon the development
and course of western civilization, nor does
any culture live so
completely in our own as
theirs.
Archaeology, the science of the past, now
is able to bring to bear the most modern
technological weapons in its search for new
light from the past for the illumination of
the present, such as, for example, the recently
developed radiocarbon dater, which counts
81

the extremely faint radioactivity of the re
maining radiocarbon in very old organic
materials such as charcoal or cloth, and, by
reference to the fact that half the original
radioactivity decays in approximately 5600
years, can thus assign an accurate date to the
material studied.
It is thus largely due to important new evi
dence discovered in recent years by archae
ology that we can now trace for the first time
the entire course of Western civilization from
its roots deep in the Orient, in the Sumerian,
Babylonian, Assyrian and Persian cultures of
the Tigris-Euphrates valley in Asia Minor,
and in the Egyptian civilization of the Nile
valley, from the most primitive days of man
in Palaeolithic and Neolithic ages, in a
continuous, unbroken stream down through
the brilliant Aegean civilization to classical
Greece, thence to Rome, on into the Middle
Ages, to Europe and the modern world. Man
is thus in a better position to understand him
self and his origins today than he has ever
been before.
What will man, what will you graduates,
do with the knowledge and understanding?
That is the important thing. During your
years in the University you have been exposed
to many influences, not the least of which has
been the liberal arts. These are the studies
whose purpose, in the words of President
Griswold of Yale University, is "to awaken
and develop intellectual and spiritual values
in the individual before he enters upon his
chosen career, so that he may bring to that
career the greatest possible assets of intelli
gence, resourcefulness, judgment, and char
acter."
The liberal arts are
traditionally and by
derivation those studies which are
becoming
to free men, and in our
present world they
have thus acquired a new and highly urgent
current connotation. In daily growing meas
ure, and from all facets of our hfe, is coming
recognition that it is the hberal arts which
lie at the roots of the greatness of our two
nations, and that liberally educated men and
women are the best�and possibly the onlyhope for the preservation of freedom in a
world which shows alarming tendencies in
many ways to retum to the uses of slavery.
Our countries need today more than ever
before men and women thus Uberally edu
cated if we are to measure
up to our
oppor
tunity and responsibility in the position of
world leadership which we now
occupy. The
challenge of today and tomorrow demands
men and women of trained intelligence, of
mental, emotional and spiritual maturity,
who have breadth of perception and depth
of understanding, who comprehend the
relevance of man's knowledge to his every
day practical problems, and who, even more
than this, are aware of the responsibility
which freedom places upon them.
Freedom is much more than freedom from
things�freedom from material want, freedom
from fear and insecurity; in the real sense
freedom exists only as freedom for something:
freedom for responsibility, for faith, for initia
tive, for man's personal fulfillment as a crea
tive individual.
Thus character, the climactic word in Presi
dent Griswold's definition, becomes the key
stone of the educational process, because
without it, intelligence and knowledge are
impotent. Man must have the mind-set, tiie
sense of values�the character�to use his
knowledge and intelligence wisely and well,
for the benefit of his fellowmen as well as
of himself, else knowledge can become per
verted to selfish ignoble, or even evil ends.
Mental brilliance and knowledge in themselves
are no
guarantee of right acting or right
living. The pages of history, even the most
recent history, are filled with examples of
intellect directed to evil purposes.
Character is the most important endproduct of education without which the en
tire process loses meaning. Nations such as
ours survive not by their material wealth
but by the uses made of it. Only by choice,
by wisdom, by direction and foresight, toler
ance and generosity, can we
prove we are
really free�and remain so.
Your lives here as members of the active
chapter of our
great fraternity can have done
much�and I sincerely hope for each of you
that this has happened�to develop in you
those qualities of heart and mind that we
call by that overworked word, character.
Your associations with your fraternal brothers
here and elsewhere in the days to come can
strengthen those qualities still further, if you
will respond. Fraternity life can be for the
individual a
priceless opportunity for experi
ence in human relations, in fellowship, in
group living, in individual and group responsi
bility, in discovering and developing qualities
of leadership, of personal conviction, of con
duct and integrity. Mere membership in
the fraternity is no
guarantee that these things
will come about for each of you; rather they

Dear Brother:
I noticed in the Spring, 1957 issue of The
Diamond that you had listed the name of my
father in the necrology section, and it occurs
to me that no one has thought to inform you
of the details of his career, nor that of his
brother, also a Psi U, and recently deceased.
Stanley Taylor Woods, Psi '13, was born
in Waterport, New York, on December 30,
1889. At Hamilton College, he was a
promi
nent athlete. He was a
partner in the Woods
and Vick Company, a coal concern, until
1933, and then an officer of the Woods and
Sprague Milling Co., Inc., (both of Albion,
New York). He died on November 8, 1955
after a
long illness, leaving his widow and
three sons, two of whom were Psi U's. Stanley
Woods was
prominent in community activities,
and therein lies his major contiibution, aside
from family considerations, to society. It would
be futile to list all of his activities, but he
will be most remembered for his contribu
tions to education through thirty years of
service on the Albion Board of Education. I
should like to quote from the remarks of
the pastor of the First Presbyterian Church
on the occasion of his funeral:
"Stanley Woods was a
prince in his human
relationships. He had that rare
gift of friend
ship, and there are hundreds of people today
who will remember his friendly and amiable
ways when they met him at the house of
God, in his home, at his place of business or
at some board meeting. I suppose there is
no one in the whole Albion area who had a
wider circle of friends than Mr. Woods.
Many a
young person received encouragement
from him and was
helped. . . ."
After his death, the family business was
carried on
by his brother, Howard Lee Woods,
Theta '15, and other members of the family.
Howard Woods was born in Albion, New York,
in 1894. Like his brother, he was a
promi
nent athlete in college (Union College,
Schenectady, New York). He served in the
fledgling air corps, U.S. Army during World
War I, and then became an officer of the
Woods and Sprague Milling Co., Inc., Albion,
New York, a
position he retained until his
sudden death in February, 1957. Howard left
a wife, but no children. He was a
lifelong
member of the Methodist church, a member
of the advisory Board of the Albion office
of the Marine Trust Company of Western
New York, and prominent in the affairs of
the New York State Millers' Society.
Sincerely,
Richard S. Woods, Upsilon '41
and for my brother,
